Signature of dissolved organic matter and microbial communities based on 
different oxygen levels response during distillers dried grains with solubles 
plus sugarcane pith co-fermentations 
Yiwu Wang a, Xiaolan Li a, Kecheng Li a, Yite Huang a, Hongxiang Yang a, Pengfei Zhu a, 
Zhanyou Chi b, Yongping Xu b, Qunliang Li a,* 
a School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Guangxi University, Nanning 530004, China 
b School of Bioengineering, Dalian University of Technology, Dalian 116024, China

G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T

A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
DDGS 
Sugarcane pith 
Co-formentation 
Microbial community 
Dissolved organic matter 
A B S T R A C T   
The objective of this study was to investigate the relationship between dissolved organic matter (DOM) and 
microbial communities during the co-fermentation of distillers dried grains with solubles (DDGS) and sugarcane 
pith at different oxygen levels. In aerobic fermentation (AF), the content of DOM decreased from 32.61 mg/g to 
14.14 mg/g, and decreased from 32.61 mg/g to 30.83 mg/g in anaerobic fermentation (ANF). Phenols and al­
cohols were consumed first in AF, while lipids and proteins were consumed first in ANF. Degradation rates of 
cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin in AF (6.67%, 39.93%, 36.50%) were higher than those in ANF (0.69%, 
18.36%, 9.12%). Firmicutes, Actinobacteriota and Ascomycota were the main phyla in community. Distance-based 
redundancy analysis showed that pH, organic matter (OM) and DOM were the main driving factors of microbial 
community succession.

1. Introduction 
Since the Industrial revolution, with the extensive use of coal, oil, 
natural gas and other fossil energy, the ecological environment of the 
earth has been destroyed. Greenhouse gas emissions pose a serious 
threat to the sustainable development of human society (Muhammad 
et al., 2014). In order to ensure national energy security, many countries 
have issued policies to encourage the development of fuel ethanol in­
dustry (Zabed et al., 2017). According to the American Renewable Fuels 
Association (RFA), China accounted for about 4.0% of the world’s fuel 
ethanol production, making it the third largest ethanol producer (Wu 
et al., 2021). The production mode of bioethanol can be divided into dry 
grinding and wet grinding, and dry grinding is the main mode of pro­
duction (Iram et al., 2021). Because of the high cost and water con­
sumption, most ethanol plants in China usually use the improved dry 
grinding method to produce ethanol. The by-product called dry dis­
tiller’s grains with solubles (DDGS) was obtained by dry grinding in the 
ethanol plant, and its rational use could improve the benefits of the corn 
ethanol refineries. 
DDGS was widely used in animal husbandry, aquaculture, and 
poultry feed because it was rich in crude protein, fat, and vitamins and 
other nutrients (Iram et al., 2020). There are anti-nutritional factors 
such as restricted amino acids and phytic acid in DDGS, which affect the 
absorption and utilization of nutrients by monogastric animals (Sun 
et al., 2021a). Solid-state fermentation was used to improve the nutri­
tional characteristics, digestibility and palatability of feed, and macro­
molecular substances and anti-nutritional factors were transformed into 
high-quality, non-toxic feed raw materials or commercial feed under the 
metabolism of natural or artificial microorganisms (Yang et al., 2021; Li 
et al., 2020a, Li et al., 2020b). At present, nitrogen-rich DDGS with 
lignocellulosic waste (rich in fermentable sugars), were co-fermented to 
produce nutrient-rich pig feed (Sun et al., 2021a). Guangxi sugar in­
dustry produces a large amount of sugarcane pith (rich in fermentable 
sugars) every year. Burning or discarding sugarcane pith directly is a 
waste of resources. Sugarcane pith can be used as the substrate of solid 
state fermentation to produce animal feed, which can increase the added 
value and protect the environment. 
Dissolved organic matter (DOM) was a complex organic mixture 
composed of amino acids, sugars, polyphenols, humus and other com­
pounds, which contains carboxyl, quinone, aldehyde and other func­
tional groups, so it could participate in adsorption, electron transfer 
reaction, microbial metabolism and chelation (Wang et al., 2014; Neb­
bioso and Piccolo, 2013). Dissolved organic matter included dissolved 
organic carbon (DOC), dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) and dissolved 
organic phosphorus (DOP). Attention to the dynamic changes of DOM is 
helpful to further understand the role of DOM in carbon, nitrogen and 
phosphorus biochemical processes. Nowadays, two-dimensional corre­
lation spectroscopy (2D-COS) played an important role in exploring the 
evolution and interaction mechanism of organic compounds at the 
molecular level. The combination of 2D-COS technology and Fourier 
Transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) has made an important contri­
bution to the study of DOM, which is helpful to analyze the structure and 
changes of DOM (Niu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2019). In addition to FTIR, 
2D-COS technology can also be used to analyze DOM in combination 
with UV–visible spectrum, fluorescence spectrum, excitation-emission 
matrix-parallel factor (EEM-PARAFAC) and Raman spectrum (Chen 
et al., 2019). In the process of aerobic composting and anaerobic 
digestion, microorganisms could use DOM to grow and reproduce, and 
microbial metabolic pathways such as glycolysis, anaerobic carbon fix­
ation, lignin decomposition and so on were also closely related to DOM 
(Li et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2019; Suominen et al, 2021; Zhu et al., 
2020). In other words, the properties of DOM affected the metabolic 
capacity of microbial communities, and the composition of dissolved 
organic matter was influenced by microbial metabolic reactions 
(Fasching et al., 2020). Under aerobic or anaerobic treatment, although 
the same raw materials are used, the system has a unique microbial 
community and biotransformation pathway, which affects the final 
product (Fernandez-Bayo et al., 2018). For example, Aspergillus and 
Bacillus subtilis secrete protease, xylanase, pectinase and so on under 
aerobic conditions, while lactic acid bacteria can produce organic acids 
under anaerobic conditions. The succession of microbial communities in 
the substrate was promoted or inhibited at different oxygen levels, 
which in turn affected the composition of DOM and ultimately the 
quality of solid fermented feed. Thus, it is necessary to compare and 
analyze the aerobic and anaerobic fermentation of DDGS and sugarcane 
pith. Studies on the relationship between DOM and microbial commu­
nity were mainly focused on the environment and composting, while 
there were few studies on solid state fermentation of animal feed. 
Therefore, in order to provide more information, the relationship be­
tween environmental factors, DOM and microbial community during 
DDGS and sugarcane pith co-fermentation under different oxygen levels 
was explored. 
The aim of this work was: (1) to use two-dimensional correlation 
spectroscopy (2D-COS) FTIR to study the change sequence of DOM 
characteristic functional groups during the co-fermentation of sugarcane 
pith and DDGS; (2) to use dynamic analysis of microbial community to 
obtained the dominant fungi and bacteria in different stages of 
fermentation;(3) to establish the relationship between physicochemical 
parameters, DOM and microbial community. This study provided a new 
idea for DDGS and sugarcane pith co-fermentation process and optimi­
zation of fermentation efficiency, and attempted to achieve reasonable 
utilization of resources and sustainable economic development. 
2. Material and methods 
2.1. Experimental procedure and materials 
Dried distiller’s grain with solubles (DDGS) and sugarcane pith were 
obtained from Weifang Ensign Industry Co., Ltd (Shandong, China) and 
Nanxu sugar factory (Nanning, China), respectively. The physicochem­
ical properties of fermentation raw materials are shown in Table 1. In 
order to obtain a suitable C/N ratio for solid state fermentation, DDGS 
was mixed with sugarcane pith at the ratio of 2:1, and the initial mois­
ture was adjusted to about 60% (Sun et al., 2021b). An average of 1.75 
kg of material was hand-packed into 5-L polyethylene terephthalate 
plastic canisters, producing a total of five plastic canisters. Four of the 
plastic tanks were sealed with three layers of polyethylene film, set as 
anaerobic fermentation (ANF). The remaining one was set as aerobic 
fermentation (AF). In this experiment, distillers dried grains with soluble 
were co-fermentation with carbon-rich sugarcane pith at an ambient 
temperature range of 18.5 ℃ to 30 ℃ for 50 d. 
During the whole aerobic fermentation process, samples were fully 
mixed and homogeneous feed samples were collected by multi-point 
sampling method at 0, 4, 16, 25 and 50 days after fermentation initia­
tion (L´opez-Gonz´alez et al., 2015). Four anaerobic fermentation tanks 
were placed for 4, 16, 25 and 50 days, respectively, and the sampling 
method was the same as that of aerobic fermentation. The samples 
extracted from aerobic fermentation and anaerobic fermentation were 
denoted as AF and ANF, respectively. Samples were frozen (-20℃) until 
further analysis.

2.2. Analysis of physicochemical parameters 
During the fermentation process, the temperature (T) and room 
temperature (RT) at three horizontal points in the center of the plastic 
tank were monitored at 12:00 noon every day. The samples were dried 
to constant weight in an oven at 80℃ to determine the moisture content, 
and then burned in a muffle furnace at 550 ℃ for 5 h to determine the 
content of organic matter (OM). The pH value of the sample extracts was 
determined by pH meter (PHS-25, China). 
2.3. Extraction and analysis of DOM 
5 g fermentation sample was placed in a conical flask, 50 mL 
deionized water was added, and shaken for 24 h. The mixture was 
centrifuged at 6,000 RPM and then filtered by a 0.45 μm membrane. (He 
et al., 2011; Li et al., 2017). The filtrate was freeze-dried and stored at 
4℃ for further analysis. The characteristics of DOM in different 
fermentation stages were obtained by using total organic carbon 
analyzer (TOC-LCPH, Shimadzu, Japan) and Fourier transform infrared 
spectroscopy (IRTracer-100, Shimadzu, Japan). According to Noda’s 
method, 2d correlation spectra were obtained by using 2Dshige, 
V.1.0.0.0 software. The synchronous correlation spectra are composed 
of autocorrelation peaks on the main diagonal and cross peaks on the 
non-diagonal, which can be used to obtain the degree of interference of 
the molecular structure and the correlation between functional groups. 
Overlapping peaks were distinguished by asynchronous correlation 
spectra, and the sequence of changes of functional groups was analyzed 
by combining two correlation spectra (Niu et al., 2021). 
2.4. Degradation analysis of lignocellulose 
Van Soest method was used to determine the content of lignocellu­
lose in fermentation samples (Van Soest et al., 1991). The value of acid 
decontaminated fiber minus the value of acid decontaminated lignin 
was the content of cellulose. The content of hemicellulose was obtained 
by subtracting the value of neutral decontamination fiber from that of 
acidic decontamination fiber. In addition, the content of lignin was 
determined by the difference between ash and acid decontamination 
fiber. 
2.5. Microbial sequencing 
FastDNA® Spin Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, USA) was used to 
extract total DNA from fermentation samples, and purity and integrity of 
DNA were detected by NanoDrop2000 and 1% AGAR gel electropho­
resis, respectively (Dineen et al., 2010). The DNA extract was stored at 
−20 ℃ for further analysis. The V3-V4 hypervariable region of 16S 
rRNA was amplified by bacterial universal primers 338F(ACTCC­
TACGGGAGGCAGCAG) and 806R (GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT). 
Fungal ITS amplicon sequencing used the ITS1F (CTTGGTCATTTA­
GAGGAAGTAA) and ITS2R (GCTGCGTTCTTCATCGATGC) universal 
primers. Then, amplified products were sent to Majorbio Bio-Pharm 
Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) for sequencing using Miseq 
PE300 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). 
2.6. Statistics analysis 
All experiments were conducted in triplicates. The physicochemical 
parameters data were analyzed by SPSS Statistics 22.0 and ORIGIN 9.0. 
On the Majorbio cloud platform (www.MajorBio.com), the distance- 
based redundancy analysis method was used to analyze the relation­
ship among environmental factors, microbial community structure and 
DOM characteristics. 
3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Analysis of physicochemical parameters of samples during 
fermentation 
Fig. 1 showed the changes of environmental factors (temperature, 
moisture, pH, OM) that affect the efficiency of DDGS and sugarcane pith 
during solid state fermentation at different oxygen levels. Temperature 
was the main factor affecting the composition of microbial communities 
during fermentation (Guan et al., 2018). As shown in Fig. 1a, mesophilic 
microorganisms used biodegradable organic matter to grow and release 
heat in the process of AF, so the temperature increased rapidly from 
26.0℃ (day 0) to 48.1℃ (day 3). Due to the degradation of organic 
matter, the temperature of the materials in the fermenter decreased 
gradually from 50.1 ℃ (day 5) to 27.85 ℃ (day 16). After 21 days of 
fermentation, the reactor temperature was basically maintained at the 
ambient temperature, indicating that the microbial activity decreased 
gradually. In the process of ANF, the temperature of the material in the 
plastic tank was basically maintained at the ambient temperature, and 
there was no obvious change. 
During the fermentation process, the change of water content in the 
culture substrate would have an important effect on the growth and 
metabolism of microorganisms. Fig. 1b showed the change in moisture 
during the fermentation process. In AF, moisture increased gradually 
from day 0 (53.33%) to day 16 (59.18%), which was slightly higher than 
that of ANF. It is worth noting that moisture of AF continued to decrease 
from day 16 to day 50 (52.91%), while moisture of ANF on day 50 
(59.76%) was higher than that of AF. During the whole fermentation 
process, whether AF or ANF, moisture was always within the range 
suitable for microbial growth (Raghavarao et al., 2003). 
Fig. 1c illustrated the change of pH during fermentation, the tends of 
AF treatment increased first and then decreased, while the tends of ANF 
treatment decreased gradually. The initial pH would affect the activity 
of microorganisms, and the growth and metabolism of microorganisms 
would affect the pH as fermentation progresses. In AF process, the pH 
value increased rapidly with the mineralization of nitrogen-containing 
organic compounds (proteins and amino acids) and decomposition of 
organic acids under the action of microorganisms (Wang et al., 2016; 
Jiang et al., 2019). Due to the release of ammonia and organic decom­
position into organic acids, the pH decreased gradually. In ANF process, 
the decrease of pH value was related to the production of organic acids. 
(Zhang et al.,2019). 
In addition, the changes of organic matter reflected the growth and 
reproduction of microorganisms in the substrate. As shown in Fig. 1d, in 
AF process, due to the degradation of OM by microorganisms, the con­
tent of OM decreased from 93.46% (day 0) to 87.68% (day 50). How­
ever, under anaerobic conditions, the reduction of OM content in ANF 
was much lower than that in AF, because the decrease of pH inhibited 
the activity of some microorganisms and reduced the degradation of 
organic matter. 
3.2. Characteristics of DOM 
3.2.1. Analysis of DOM content 
In the process of fermentation, DOM dissolved in the liquid film at 
the interface between gas and solid, which could be directly absorbed 
and utilized by microorganisms to drive microbial community succes­
sion (Fernandez-Bayo et al., 2018). The variation trend of DOM content 
during DDGS and sugarcane pith co-fermentation on different oxygen 
levels were shown in Fig. 2a. At the beginning of fermentation, the 
content of DOM decreased from 32.61 mg/g (day 0) to 23.87 mg/g (day 
4) in AF process, owing to DOM can be directly consumed by microor­
ganisms and converted into other metabolites. The content of DOM on 
day 16 was higher than that on day 4, because lignocellulose and other 
refractory organic matter could be converted into DOM. Then, the 
content of DOM decreased to 14.14 mg/g on day 50. Compared with AF,

of DDGS and sugarcane pith at different oxygen levels (Fig. 2), the

transformation of DOM functional groups was more significant in Fig. 2b 
and weaker in Fig. 2c. Therefore, DOM changed more significantly in the 
presence of oxygen. All the cross peaks in the AF and ANF synchroni­
zation diagrams are positive, indicating that they were in the same di­
rection of change. In detail, there were five main automatic peaks in the 
figure, located at 3400, 2923, 1645, 1407 and 1040 cm−1, respectively, 
while the peak was at 3400 cm−1 was the most significant. The energy 
band near 3400 cm−1 may be due to O–H bonds. In addition, most 
automatic peaks on asynchronous maps have a plus or minus sign, 
indicating that DOM was also generated when DOM was consumed. 
Combined with the corresponding negative cross peaks in the AF asyn­
chronous mapping, the structural change order of DOM functional 
groups was inferred: 3400 cm−1 > 2923 cm−1 > 1645 cm−1 > 1040 
cm−1 > 1407 cm−1, corresponding to O–H stretch vibration of hydroxyl 
groups(El Fels et al.,2014) > aliphatic C–H bond stretching vibration 
(Soobhany et al.,2017) > aromatic compound C = C bond stretching 
vibration (Zhu et al.,2020) > C-O bond stretching vibration of poly­
saccharides or polysaccharide–like substances (Zhang et al.,2014) >
COO– symmetric stretching and CH3 bending vibrations: lipids, proteins 
(Aksoy and Severcan, 2012). Combined with the corresponding negative 
cross peaks in the ANF asynchronous mapping, the structural change 
order of DOM functional groups was inferred: 1407 cm−1 > 1040 cm−1 
> 1645 cm−1 > 2923 cm−1 > 3400 cm−1, which corresponds to COO– 
symmetric stretching and CH3 bending vibrations: lipids, proteins 
(Aksoy and Severcan, 2012) > C-O bond stretching vibration of poly­
saccharides or polysaccharide–like substances (Zhang et al.,2014) >
stretching vibration of aromatic C = C bond (Zhu et al.,2020) > aliphatic 
C–H bond stretching vibration (Soobhany et al.,2017) > O–H stretch 
vibration of hydroxyl groups (El Fels et al.,2014). 
To summarize, in the process of AF, phenols and alcohols in DOM 
were consumed first, followed by aliphatic, aromatic compounds, sugars 
and carbohydrates, and lipids and proteins. In the process of ANF, lipids 
and proteins in DOM were consumed first, followed by sugars and car­
bohydrates, aromatic compounds, aliphatic compounds, phenols and 
alcohols. 
3.3. Degradation of lignocellulose 
The special structure of lignin hindered the contact of microorgan­
isms with cellulose and hemicellulose, so the degradation of lignocel­
lulose became difficult (Wang et al., 2021). As shown in Fig. 3c, there 
was a significant difference in lignocellulose degradation between AF 
and ANF during co-fermentation of DDGS and sugarcane pith. Although 
at the initial stage of fermentation, the lignin degradation rate of AF was 
lower than that of ANF. However, with the extension of fermentation 
time, the lignin degradation rate of AF was significantly higher than that 
of ANF. After day 50, the lignin degradation rate of AF reached 36.50%. 
The accessibility of cellulase to lignocellulose increased significantly 
with the destruction of lignin structure (Wang et al., 2021). As a result, 
the degradation rates of cellulose and hemicellulose in AF were higher 
than those in ANF, which was consistent with the changes in Fig. 3a and 
3b. In the process of microbial community succession, lignin was 
degraded into phenols and quinones, and cellulose was degraded into 
polysaccharides and monosaccharides, providing carbon and energy 
sources for microbial growth. Similarly, hemicellulose could also be 
absorbed and metabolized by microorganisms (Ma et al., 2020). The 
results showed that the microorganisms in the mixture of DDGS and 
sugarcane pith had stronger ability to degrade lignocellulose in AF,

which was contrary to ANF. The degradation of lignocellulose led to the 
increase of DOM content, which was consistent with the change of DOM 
in 16 days. The purpose of this study was to compare the fermentation 
conditions of DDGS and sugarcane pith under different oxygen levels. 
According to the results, the fermentation with the endogenous micro­
organisms in the substrate has achieved certain effect, and the next step 
is to add some candidate strains fermentation (Sun et al., 2021b). 
3.4. Microbial community analysis 
3.4.1. Dynamics of bacterial community during co-fermentation 
Fig. 4a showed the changes of phylum level bacterial communities 
during the co-fermentation of sugarcane pith and DDGS at different 
oxygen levels. At the initial stage, Firmicutes, Actinobacteriota, Proteo­
bacteria and Bacteroidota were the dominant phyla in the fermentation 
process. During AF, the abundance of Firmicutes increased from day 
0 (25.90%) to day 4 (98.32%) and decreased from day 4 (98.32%) to day 
50 (8.64%). Liu et al., (2018) proved that Firmicutes can degrade 
lignocellulose and hydrolyze polysaccharides. Therefore, the change of 
Firmicutes’ abundance resulted in the change of lignocellulose degra­
dation rate during AF (Fig. 3). During ANF, the abundance of Firmicutes 
increased gradually from day 0 (25.90%) to day 50 (90.82%). Therefore, 
the degradation of lignocellulose in ANF process was relatively slow. 
During the AF process, Actinobacteriota decreased from 51.58% (day 0) 
to 0.71% (day 4), and then increased to 53.50% (day 50). Actino­
bacteriotas were mesophilic or thermophilic that participated in the 
degradation of lignocellulose residues, but only a small part of Actino­
bacteriota can tolerate high temperature during fermentation (Zhao 
et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2020). In the ANF process, Actinobacteriota 
decreased from 51.58% (day 0) to 5.63% (day 50). The abundance of 
Actinobacteriota in AF was higher than that in ANF, resulting in a higher 
degradation rate of lignocellulose in AF. However, high microbial ac­
tivity resulted in more DOM consumption in AF and reduced the nutri­
tional value of fermentation products. 
The changes of bacterial community at species level during co- 
fermentation of sugarcane pith and DDGS on different oxygen levels 
were shown in Fig. 4b. During AF, the abundance of Bacillus ginsengihumi 
increased from day 0 (3.32%) to day 4 (59.00%) and decreased from day 
4 (59.00%) to day 50 (0.89%). The abundance of Bacillus ginsengihumi 
was the highest in AF on day 4, and that of Bacillus ginsengihumi was 
inhibited in ANF. Bacillus ginsengihumi could secrete phytase, which 
hydrolyzed phytic acid into inorganic phosphate and a small amount of 
phosphorylated inositol derivatives (Toymentseva et al., 2015; Trosha­
gina et al., 2018). As a result, Bacillus ginsengihumi with high abundance 
was beneficial to the degradation of phytate phosphorus in DDGS and 
the digestion of DDGS feed by single-stomach animals, which improved 
the nutritional value of DDGS feed. In AF process, the abundance of 
Lactobacillus plantarum was always<0.15%, while in ANF process, the 
abundance of Lactobacillus plantarum increased gradually from day 0 
(0.005%) to day 50(18.71%). Anaerobic environment and low pH were 
favorable for the growth of Lactobacillus plantarum. Lactobacillus plan­
tarum had a high survival rate in acidic environment and could regulate 
intestinal flora and immune response of piglets. In addition, Lactobacillus 
plantarum could also secrete phytase, which had the ability to promote 
phytic acid degradation in DDGS (Dell’Anno et al., 2021; Shin et al., 
2019; Sumengen et al., 2013; ´Sli˙zewska et al., 2021). In AF, the abun­
dance of Bacillus coagulans increased from day 0 (0.38%) to day 4 
(30.49%) and decreased from day 4 (30.49%) to day 50 (0.87%). The 
abundance of Bacillus coagulans was the highest on day 4, then decreased 
with the extension of fermentation time. In ANF, the abundance of Ba­
cillus coagulans was always lower than 1.55%. Bacillus coagulans was a 
spore producing strain with high temperature resistance and charac­
teristics of Bacillus and Lactobacillus, which has important application 
value in food industry. In addition, Bacillus coagulans improved growth 
performance of piglets by promoting intestinal barrier function and was 
a potential substitute for antibiotic growth promoters (Konuray and 
Erginkaya, 2018; Fu et al., 2021). Consequently, short-term AF 
fermentation was beneficial to increase the abundance of Bacillus

coagulans and may improve the quality of feed. To sum up, short-term 
fermentation was beneficial to the growth of probiotics Bacillus ginsen­
gihumi and Bacillus coagulans in AF (day 0-day 4), while long-term 
fermentation was beneficial to the growth of probiotics Lactobacillus 
plantarum in ANF (day 0-day 50). 
3.4.2. Dynamics of fungal community during co-fermentation 
The changes of phylum level fungal community during co- 
fermentation of sugarcane pith and DDGS at different oxygen levels 
were shown in Fig. 4c. At the beginning of fermentation, Ascomycota 
(51.08%) and Basidiomycota (48.69%) were the dominant phyla in the 
fungal community. In AF, Ascomycota was always the dominant phylum 
in the fermentation process, accounting for>99% of the total observed 
sequences. Different from AF, the abundance of Ascomycota in ANF 
gradually increased from day 0 (51.08%) to day 4 (98.96%) and 
decreased from day 4 (98.96%) to day 50 (87.91%). The abundance of 
Basidiomycota decreased gradually from day 0 (48.69%) to day 4 
(1.03%), and increased slightly from day 4 (1.03%) to day 50 (11.69%). 
Therefore, Ascomycota was always the dominant fungal in the fermen­
tation process under different oxygen levels. 
The changes of fungal community at species level during co- 
fermentation of sugarcane pith and DDGS at different oxygen levels 
were shown in Fig. 4d. In the initial stage of fermentation, Burgoa sp 
(31.42%), Byssochlamys spectabilis (18.45%) and unclassified Talaromyces 
(11.11%) were the dominant bacteria in the fermentation samples. With 
the prolongation of fermentation time, the dominant species changed 
significantly during fermentation. In AF, the abundance of Issatchenkia 
orientalis increased from day 0 (0.00%) to day 4 (4.55%), then gradually 
decreased to day 50 (0.54%). In ANF, the abundance of Issatchenkia 
orientalis increased from day 0 (0.005%) to day 25 (67.82%), and then 
gradually decreased to day 50 (50.75%). Issatchenkia orientalis was a 
kind of non-yeast with multiple tolerance (for example, acetic acid 
tolerance, high heat, and salt tolerance) and had potential in wine 
making and bioethanol production (Li et al., 2020a, Li et al., 2020b). 
Therefore, in ANF, an increase in the abundance of Issatchenkia orientalis 
may produce a large amount of ethanol. In AF, the abundance of 
Aspergillus fumigatus was low in the first four days (≤0.04%), but with 
the extension of fermentation time, the abundance of Aspergillus fumi­
gatus increased, which was not conducive to the health of animals. In 
ANF, Aspergillus fumigatus abundance was low, with day 50 (3.75%) 
reaching its maximum. The results showed that the control of fermen­
tation time was beneficial to reduce the pollution of feed products. In 
AF, the abundance of Diutina rugosa increased from day 0 (0.22%) to day 
4 (32.09%) and then decreased to day 50 (12.21%). In ANF, the abun­
dance of Diutina rugosa increased from day 0 (0.22%) to day 4 (10.96%), 
then gradually decreased to day 50 (1.31%). Diutina rugosa can be used 
as a feed additive to regulate immunity and promote the growth of 
broilers (Wang et al., 2019). In AF, the abundance of Candida tropicalis 
gradually increased from day 0 (0.003%) to day 50 (13.28%), while in 
ANF, the abundance of Candida tropicalis gradually increased from day 
0 (0.003%) to day 4 (7.63%) and decreased from day 4 (7.63%) to day 
50 (1.65%). Candida tropicalis had the ability to produce extracellular 
phytase (Suryani et al., 2021). Therefore, Candida Tropicalis was bene­
ficial to the degradation of phytic acid in DDGS. 
3.5. Distance-based redundancy analysis 
As shown in Fig. 5, the relationship between environmental factors 
(temperature, moisture, pH, OM, DOM) and microbial communities 
(bacteria and fungi) at species level was investigated by distance-based 
redundancy analysis. The factor that has the great influence on bacterial 
community and species distribution was pH (R = 0.8505, P < 0.01), 
followed by OM (R = 0.6576, P < 0.05), DOM (R = 0.6465, P < 0.05), 
moisture and temperature, as shown in Fig. 5a. Specifically, DOM was 
positively correlated with OM, but negatively correlated with pH, 
moisture and temperature, indicating that DOM was consumed by mi­
croorganisms with the degradation of organic matter, and the increase of 
temperature, pH and moisture resulted in the decrease of DOM. In 
addition, the relationship between bacterial species and environmental 
factors in the first five abundances was analyzed, and it was considered 
that environmental factors had great effects on Bacillus ginsengihumi and 
Lactobacillus plantarum. Bacillus ginsengihumi was positively correlated 
with temperature and pH, indicating that the increase of temperature 
and pH value in the middle and early stage of AF was beneficial to the 
activity of Bacillus ginsengihumi. Lactobacillus plantarum was positively 
correlated with moisture, indicating that the increase of moisture in ANF 
was beneficial to the growth of Lactobacillus plantarum. In conclusion, 
organic matter produced soluble organic matter under the metabolism 
of bacterial community, but moisture, temperature and pH value 
affected the abundance of bacterial community and indirectly affected 
the characteristics of DOM. In addition, the growth and metabolism of 
microorganisms also consumed part of DOM, which resulted in the di­
versity of DOM content and functional groups. 
In order to explore the relationship between microorganisms and 
environmental factors in more detail, fungal communities were also 
discussed. As shown in Fig. 5b, the factor that has great influence on 
fungal community and species distribution was pH (R = 0.6308, P <
0.05), followed by DOM (R = 0.6223, P < 0.05), OM, moisture and 
temperature. In detail, DOM was positively correlated with OM, mois­
ture, and negatively correlated with pH and temperature. Interestingly,

it was slightly different from the correlation of the above bacterial 
communities. The relationship between the top five fungi species and

the increase of pH and temperature would inhibit the abundance of 
Issatchenkia orientalis and control the generation of DOM. 
4. Conclusions 
This study revealed that ANF was beneficial to the preservation of 
DOM content during fermentation process. Phenols and alcohols were 
consumed first in AF, while lipids and proteins were consumed first in 
ANF. Bacillus ginsengihumi and Issatchenkia orientalis played an important 
role in the degradation of OM and the formation of DOM. In addition, 
the main environmental factors driving the microbial community were 
pH, OM and DOM in the process of fermentation. In summary, these 
findings provided some novel insights into the signature of dissolved 
organic matter and relevant microbiome during the co-fermentation of 
DDGS and sugarcane pith.
